#| label: footer-options

We validate inference with simulation-based calibration (SBC) [@cook_validation_2006; @talts_validating_2020].
[Performance checks](performance_checks.html) hold the truth at one value and measure how far the estimates land from it, while SBC draws a new truth for every replicate and checks the posterior as a whole.

For prior SBC, replicates draw parameters from the prior, simulate a study at them, fit it back with the same model, and rank each drawn value among the posterior draws of its fit.
When the likelihood and the sampler are correct, the drawn value behaves as one more posterior draw, so its rank is uniform over the replicates.

We use the same final-size example presented in [Get started](housepi.html):

```{r}
#| label: model-setup
# define the model as in 'Get Started'
library(housepi)
set_housepi_theme(colour_strips = TRUE)
set.seed(42)

hh_model <- flu_1918_frederick |>
  new_housepi_model("final-size") |>
  add_parameter(import = "template")

get_parameters(hh_model)
```

The true parameters of each replicate are drawn from the priors of imported definitions.
The check needs no fit to the data, which is only used to pass the household structure to the simulations.

# Rank the prior draws

`check_calibration()` simulates each study on the households of Frederick, as calibration conditions on the design of the study.
Each fit runs the default MCMC configuration of `run_inference()`, which returns 800 draws, here on two threads.
The drawn value is ranked among 99 draws thinned evenly from these 800, so its rank takes one of `rank_levels = 100` values (0 to 99):

```{r}
#| label: calibration
calibration <- hh_model |>
  check_calibration(nrep = 100, threads = 2, rank_levels = 100)
calibration

# overview of the sweep, averaged over replicates
calibration$overview
```

A rank is uniform only if the draws it is taken among behave like independent ones.
A parameter is flagged when its fit fails the convergence diagnostics [@vehtari_rank_normalization_2021].
`r if (length(calibration$overview$n_flagged)) paste("Here the diagnostics flagged", calibration$overview$n_flagged, "out of", calibration$nrep, "replicates.")`

The check also ranks the log-likelihood `log_lik` of each simulated study.
A fit that ignores data would return the prior as its posterior, keeping the parameter ranks uniform.
Ranking `log_lik` as well catches that mismatch [@modrak_simulation_2025].

The rank of every parameter and of the log-likelihood in every replicate is stored in `calibration$estimates`.
Uniform ranks fill each bin of ten ranks with about `r calibration$nrep / 10` replicates:

```{r}
#| label: rank-histogram
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Four histograms, one per parameter and one for the log-likelihood,
#|  of the ranks of the drawn values among 99 posterior draws, in bins of
#|  ten ranks, against a horizontal line at the count expected for uniform
#|  ranks.
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(calibration$estimates, aes(x = rank)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10, boundary = 0, closed = "left") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = calibration$nrep / 10, colour = "coral") +
  facet_wrap(~ variable) +
  labs(x = "rank", y = "replicates")
```

Where the ranks pile up tells how the posterior is off:

- at both ends, it is too narrow, so the truth falls in its tails too often,
- in the middle, it is too wide,
- on one side, it is shifted.

Low ranks put the truth below most posterior draws, so the posterior overestimates the parameter.

# Test for uniformity

```{r}
#| label: bin-counts
#| include: false
bins <- table(calibration$estimates$variable, calibration$estimates$rank %/% 10)
```

With 100 replicates a bin of ten ranks holds 10 on average, give or take 3, and the picture changes with the bin width.
Here the bins hold from `r min(bins)` to `r max(bins)` ranks.
@sailynoja_graphical_2022 instead compare the empirical CDF of the ranks with the uniform CDF, inside a band that a uniform ECDF stays within at every point at once with 95% probability.
bayesplot draws this band with `ppc_pit_ecdf_grouped()`, from the ranks rescaled to $[0, 1]$:

```{r}
#| label: rank-ecdf
#| fig-height: 5
#| message: false
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Four panels, one per parameter and one for the log-likelihood.
#|  Each shows the difference between the empirical CDF of the scaled ranks
#|  and the uniform CDF, as a solid step line, inside a dashed band around zero.
rank_levels <- calibration$rank_levels

bayesplot::ppc_pit_ecdf_grouped(
  pit = calibration$estimates$rank / (rank_levels - 1),
  group = calibration$estimates$variable,
  K = rank_levels, prob = 0.95, plot_diff = TRUE
)
```

A posterior that overestimates puts the curve above zero, since low ranks make the ECDF rise early, and one that underestimates puts it below.
A posterior too narrow draws an S, above zero on the left and below on the right.
One too wide draws the mirror image.

`calibration$summarise()` reads the same test: `uniform` is `FALSE` when the ECDF leaves the band at any point, which happens to uniform ranks in at most 5% of checks.

```{r}
#| label: summary
calibration$summarise()
```

```{r}
#| label: verdict
#| include: false
verdict <- calibration$summarise()
n_uniform <- sum(verdict$uniform)
```

Here the test passes for `r n_uniform` of `r nrow(verdict)` ranked quantities.
Passing says that the sampler and the likelihood agree with the prior and the model.
It says nothing about whether the model fits Frederick.
For that, compare its predictions with the data in [Predictive checks](predictive_checks.html).

# Parameter recovery

Each replicate also stores the point estimate and the credible interval of its fit.
Plotted against the values the studies were simulated at, they show the parameter recovery of the run [@sailynoja_posterior_2026]:

```{r}
#| label: recovery-plot
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Four panels, one per parameter and one for the log-likelihood.
#|  Each shows one credible interval per replicate, centred on its estimate
#|  and placed at the drawn value, around the diagonal where the two are equal.
recovery_plot <- function(estimates) {
  ggplot(estimates, aes(x = truth, y = estimate)) +
    geom_abline(colour = "coral") +
    geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = cri_lower, ymax = cri_upper), size = 0.2) +
    facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free") +
    labs(x = "drawn value", y = "estimate")
}
recovery_plot(calibration$estimates)
```

Points close to the diagonal mean that a study the size of Frederick pins the parameter down.
Points pulled toward the centre of the prior mean that the study says little about it, and the posterior falls back on the prior.
That pull does not break calibration, which the ranks test.
The plot shows how much each study informs each parameter, over the whole prior, where a [performance check](performance_checks.html) looks at one value only.

# A sampler run too short

Calibration also catches a sampler run too short for its draws to stand for the posterior.
We repeat the check with two chains of 50 steps, the first 25 of each spent adapting the proposals, and keep every draw:

```{r}
#| label: short-chains
short <- hh_model |>
  check_calibration(nrep = 100, steps = 50, thin = 1, adapt = 25,
                    chains = 2, threads = 2)
short_summary <- short$summarise()
short_summary
```

```{r}
#| label: short-chains-ecdf
#| fig-height: 5
#| message: false
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Same four panels as above, for the ranks of the short chains.
bayesplot::ppc_pit_ecdf_grouped(
  pit = short$estimates$rank / (rank_levels - 1),
  group = short$estimates$variable,
  K = rank_levels, prob = 0.95, plot_diff = TRUE
)
```

```{r}
#| label: short-verdict
#| include: false
code_words <- \(x) knitr::combine_words(x, before = "`")
failed <- short_summary$variable[!short_summary$uniform]
passed <- short_summary$variable[short_summary$uniform]
extreme <- with(short$estimates,
                tapply(rank %in% c(0, rank_levels - 1), variable, mean))
```

The diagnostics flag `r sum(short$replicates$flagged)` of `r short$nrep` replicates, since 100 correlated draws are worth far fewer than 99 independent ones.
Correlated draws sit closer together than the posterior they come from, so the truth falls outside all of them too often.
Rank 0 or 99 takes `r knitr::combine_words(paste0(round(100 * extreme), "% of the ranks of \x60", names(extreme), "\x60"))`, against 2% for uniform ranks.
`r if (length(failed)) paste("The ranks of", code_words(failed), "fail the test.", "Their ECDF jumps at both ends and draws the S of a posterior too narrow, an excess that the first and last bins of a histogram would dilute among ten ranks each.")`
`r if (length(passed)) paste("The ranks of", code_words(passed), "pass on flagged fits, which is no evidence of calibration.")`

# Calibrate on the data

The checks above average over the prior.
Most truths drawn from the uniform priors of `alpha`, `beta` and `gamma` lie far from the values the Frederick data supports.
Inference can be calibrated on average over the prior and still fail where the posterior of Frederick puts its mass, or fail somewhere the data rules out [@sailynoja_posterior_2026].

Posterior calibration conditions the check on the data.
Each replicate takes one posterior draw of the Frederick fit as its truth, simulates a study at it, and fits that study together with the Frederick households.
The truth is then one more draw of the posterior given both, so its rank among the draws of that fit is uniform when inference is correct.
Passing `draws` to `check_calibration()` runs it:

```{r}
#| label: posterior-calibration
hh_fit <- run_inference(hh_model, threads = 2)
posterior_calibration <- hh_model |>
  check_calibration(hh_fit, nrep = 100, threads = 2)
posterior_calibration
```

The truths are 100 distinct posterior draws, picked evenly among the draws of the fit thinned to their effective sample size, so the fit must hold at least 100 independent draws.
Each replicate fits twice as many households as Frederick has, the observed ones plus as many simulated, so it costs more than a replicate of the prior check.
We test the ranks the same way:

```{r}
#| label: posterior-ecdf
#| fig-height: 5
#| message: false
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Same four panels as above, for the ranks of the posterior draws.
bayesplot::ppc_pit_ecdf_grouped(
  pit = posterior_calibration$estimates$rank / (rank_levels - 1),
  group = posterior_calibration$estimates$variable,
  K = rank_levels, prob = 0.95, plot_diff = TRUE
)

posterior_calibration$summarise()
```

```{r}
#| label: posterior-verdict
#| include: false
posterior_verdict <- posterior_calibration$summarise()
```

Here the test passes for `r sum(posterior_verdict$uniform)` of `r nrow(posterior_verdict)` ranked quantities.

We plot the recovery the same way:

```{r}
#| label: posterior-recovery-plot
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Same four panels as the first recovery plot, for the posterior draws.
recovery_plot(posterior_calibration$estimates)
```

The drawn values span only the posterior of Frederick, and each fit sees the Frederick households next to the simulated ones, so the points gather in a narrow range.
How far they follow the diagonal shows what the simulated households add to the observed ones.
